searches.displayName: Metabolite levels
searches.description:
Find compounds with variation in metabolite levels. Note that when the compound has multiple isotopomers, the metabolite isotopomers levels were summed.

Infected RBCs were enriched using Percoll and parasites were isolated from infected RBCs with saponin. Intracellular metabolites were measured from pellets while secreted metabolites were measured from the media
Infected RBCs, isolated parasites, and uninfected RBCs were incubated for 4 hours in RPMI containing U-13 C glutamine at pH 6.4, 7.4, and 8.4. Extracts were analyzed by mass spectrometry. The effect of pH on steady-state metabolite levels and glutamine metabolism was measured.

Warning: all metabolite assignments provided in this alpha release should be treated as preliminary.
searches.summary: Find compounds by metabolite levels

searches.displayName: LoginStats
searches.description:
Report on how many users registered and how many users logged in during the time period.

If a user logs in more than once during the time period, we only count once for that user.

Because users commonly stay logged in for many months, this report does *not* tell us how many are currently logged in. It only tells us how many went through the log in process during the time period.

The stats are gathered from the account database and the account service logs.
searches.summary: Report on how many users logged in, and how many registered.

transcript.displayName: Genomic Location
transcript.description:
Find genes that are located within a specified genomic region. Use either the Chromosome Tab or Sequence ID Tab to define the genomic location you wish to query. The search returns all genes found within your specified genomic location.

Chromosome Tab:
First select the Organism and Chromosome that you want to query. Then indicate the boundaries of the genomic location by entering the Start and End nucleotide coordinates of your region. Choosing Start=1 and End=0 will retrieve all genes on the chromosome.

Sequence ID Tab:
First enter the Genomic Sequence ID of the contig or chromosome that you want to query. Example genomic sequence IDs are: Pf3D7_04_v3, AABL01000036, PviS_CM000452, berg12. Then indicate the boundaries of the genomic location by entering the Start and End nucleotide coordinates of your region. Choosing Start=1 and End=0 will retrieve all genes on the genomic sequence.
transcript.summary: Find genes within a given genomic region such as a chromosome, scaffold or supercontig.

transcript.displayName: RNA-Seq Differential Expression (User Datasets)
transcript.description:
Find genes that are differentially expressed between two groups of samples in an RNA-Seq experiment. This search uses a guided notebook within ${projectName} that runs DESeq2, a widely-used statistical method for RNA-Seq differential expression analysis (Love et al., 2014).

How to run this search: Open the Configure Search tab and work through the notebook steps in order:
  • Select Expression Data — Choose the gene identifier variable and count type for the dataset.
  • Explore Sample Variation (optional) — Run a PCA to visualise sources of variation across samples. Use it to spot outliers or batch effects and exclude them before the DESeq2 step.
  • Define Sample Groups — Select a metadata variable (e.g. treatment, tissue type, or developmental stage) and assign samples to a Reference group and a Comparison group.
  • Set Thresholds — Explore the results on an interactive volcano plot. Adjust the effect size and p-value thresholds to highlight the genes you want to retrieve.
  • Run the Search — Click Get Answer to retrieve all genes that meet your criteria.

Effect size: The effect size is expressed as a log2 fold change — how much more or less a gene is expressed in the Comparison group relative to the Reference group. A positive value indicates up-regulation; a negative value indicates down-regulation.

P-value: DESeq2 computes both a raw p-value and a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value for each gene. The volcano plot is drawn using the raw p-value (on a −log10 scale), and the p-value threshold you set on the plot is also applied to the raw p-value. Adjusted p-values are available in the mouse-over tooltip for each point on the volcano plot. A lower p-value (raw or adjusted) indicates a more statistically confident call.

Removing outliers: If the PCA plot reveals samples that cluster away from the rest (potential outliers or contaminated libraries), you can exclude them using the Select Samples step at the top of the notebook. Apply a filter on the sample identifier or a metadata variable to remove those samples before running DESeq2. Note that changing the sample subset will reset any group assignments you have already made in the DESeq2 step, so it is best to check the PCA first before defining your groups.

transcript.displayName: Unannotated Intron Junctions
transcript.description:
This search identifies genes that contain, or are flanked by, unannotated introns – defined as RNAseq reads that map to discontinuous regions on the same DNA strand as a gene, span canonical splice donor & acceptor motifs, and are not reflected in the reference annotation for that gene. These introns may suggest incorrect gene model annotation or alternatively-spliced transcripts, and should be carefully reviewed in the genome browser, in the context of additional evidence (abundance in various samples, frequency of splicing relative to flanking exon sequences, etc). Changes to the gene model can then be made using the Apollo annotation system, if warranted. Note that clicking on individual introns in the genome browser displays a table providing much relevant information.

Search Parameters:

"Consider 5' & 3' Flanking Sequence up to (bp)" expands the query beyond annotated gene model boundaries, enabling the identification of up- or down-stream introns that may have been missed in the reference annotation.

"Minimum number of unique reads >=" controls the number of intron-spanning reads (ISRs) that must support an unannotated intron before the gene is returned by the search. Introns with low abundance relative to the total number of reads mapping to a region may not be biologically significant.

"Percent of most abundant intron" defines unannotated introns in comparison to the most abundant intron (MAI) associated with that gene. Introns mistakenly omitted from the annotated gene model are likely to be as abundant as correctly annotated introns; alternative splice variants may be observed at ~20-80%, but you may not be interested in rare 'typographical errors' made by the splicing machinery.
transcript.summary: Find genes that have high confidence novel intron junction spanning RNASequencing reads.

transcript.displayName: SNV Characteristics Within a Group of Samples
transcript.description:
Search for genes containing SNPs with certain characteristics: high SNP density, specific type or class of SNPs, high ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous SNPs, etc.
  • These statistics are computed over the samples you select, so they change with your sample set and are not comparable to the precomputed values on the gene record page or in the "Short Variant Characteristics" search.
  • In this search, SNPs are defined as sequence differences between the selected strains. If you want to include sequence differences between the selected genomes and the reference genome, then also select the reference strain.
  • Leave the default settings to obtain genes with any type of SNP. On the Results page, you can sort by many of these parameters (e.g., number of SNPs, non-synonymous/synonymous ratio, etc).
  • To obtain genes containing SNPs of a specific class (e.g., nonsense), then select "Nonsense" in the "SNP Class" and change "Number of SNPs of above class >=" to "1" (or higher).
  • As an example, running this search to compare 3D7 and Dd2 using default parameters returns 2577 genes. Among the top 20 on the list are CLAG, AMA1, chloroquine resistance marker and multiple PfEMP1 and SURFIN genes.
  • The dN/dS ratio reported here IS normalized by synonymous and nonsynonymous site counts, derived from the genetic code over the gene's representative transcript, so it does not carry the codon-bias inflation that a raw count ratio does.
  • It remains a count ratio: a variant seen in one sample weights the same as one at 50% frequency. For a frequency-weighted piN/piS across every sample loaded, use the "Short Variant Characteristics" search.
transcript.summary: Find genes which have SNPs generated by HTS sequencing meeting specific criteria (Non-synonymous / synonymous SNP ratio, SNP density, etc).

This is a count ratio - it weights a rare variant the same as a common one - so it will not equal the piN/piS in the Short Variant Characteristics search.

transcript.displayName: Short Variant Characteristics
transcript.description:
Search genes by the variation statistics summarized across every sample loaded for the organism. Short variants are single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and short insertions/deletions (Indels); both are counted in the variant totals and in the impact and effect-class statistics, while the diversity ratios (piN/piS and nucleotide diversity) rest on SNPs only, since they are computed from synonymous and nonsynonymous codon changes. These are the same numbers shown in the Genetic Variation section of the gene record page, so a gene found here will report the same values when you open it.
  • This search does not take a sample set. If you want to compare a group of samples you chose - or two groups against each other - use the "SNV Characteristics Within a Group of Samples" search instead. That one recomputes from the raw alignments and takes read-frequency and percent-called thresholds; this one reads precomputed values and returns immediately.
  • Pick an organism first. The distributions in the filter are drawn from that organism's genes, and variant density differs by an order of magnitude between organisms, so a pooled distribution would not help you choose a threshold for either.
  • Some statistics are only defined when enough alleles were sampled at a locus - common and singleton counts, highest minor allele frequency, and the diversity ratios. Where an organism's sampling does not reach that floor the value is left empty rather than reported as zero, so those genes are simply absent from that statistic's distribution. They are excluded from your result only if you filter on that statistic.
  • piN/piS is normalized by Nei-Gojobori site counts derived from the genetic code, so it does not carry the codon-bias distortion that the older non-synonymous / synonymous count ratio does. Below 1 suggests purifying selection; above 1 suggests diversifying selection.
transcript.summary:
Find genes whose precomputed variant statistics meet your criteria - variant
          density, missense and loss-of-function counts, allele frequency, or piN/piS.

transcript.displayName: Mass Spec. Evidence
transcript.description:
Find genes that have evidence for protein-level expression from mass specrtometry-based proteomics experiments.

PlasmoDB maps peptides from proteomics experiments to a reference genome and allows you to search for genes based on that mapping. Expand the Experiment/Samples parameter to see a list of proteomics datasets integrated into PlasmoDB. The list is organized by:

  1. the organism that the peptides are mapped to
  2. the experiment name (model organism)
  3. the samples analyzed in the experiment
The stringency of the search can be adjusted using the "Minimum Number of Spectera / Sample" and "Minimum Number of Unique Peptide Sequences".
Minimum Number of Spectra / Sample:
Use this parameter to set a minimum for the number of mass spectra that must support a sample (all peptides) before a gene is returned for this sample (note that this number is the sum of spectra for all peptides / sample). This parameter can be considered a measure of protein abundance within a particular sample.

Minimum Number of Unique Peptide Sequences:
Use this parameter to define the number of unique peptides that must map to a gene before the gene is returned by the search. Although protein expression is confirmed with the mapping of one unique pepetide, requiring more than one peptide to map to a gene will ensure that false positives are not returned by the search. Note that the next parameter controls whether to apply this number per sample or across all samples.

Apply min # peptide sequences / sample OR across samples:
Select Per Sample to require that each sample meet this minimum number of unique peptide sequences. Selecting All will first union the unique peptides for all selected samples and this set will be used to meet the minimum number of unique peptide sequences.
transcript.summary: Find genes that have evidence for protein-level expression from mass specrtometry-based proteomics experiments.

transcript.displayName: Epitope Presence (IEDB)
transcript.description:
Find genes whose protein products show similarity to an epitope identified by the Immune Epitope Database and Analysis Resource IEDB.

Epitopes are antigenic determinants that are part of antigens recognized by the immune system's antibodies, B-cells or T-cells. The Epitopes from the IEDB were mapped to all reference strains foud PlasmoDB to determine the identity of a specific peptide to a refrence protein.

Epitope sequences are mapped to genes (Proteins) in VEuPathDB using exact string matching or high quality BLAST similarity between the GenBank proteins listed on IEDB and the proteins of the reference strains found in PlasmoDB.

For each Epitope it is determined:

  • If IEDB peptide source protein is the same as the reference protein it is being compared to.
  • Weather peptide source protein and reference is compared to is from the same taxon.
  • Are there any mismatches between the peptide and region it matches to on the reference protein.

    A filter can be set to determine exact pepitide protein match, taxon match and if protein and peptide source protein are the same.

Find genes whose protein products are predicted to contain epitopes 
           identified by the Immune Epitope Database and Analysis Resource (IEDB).

transcript.displayName: BLAST
transcript.description:
Find genes that have BLAST similarity to your input sequence.

As of 3 Feb 2014, this search uses NCBI-BLAST to determine sequence similarity. Prior versions of the search used WU-BLAST. See the NCBI-BLAST help for more information.

First use the Target Data Type parameter to indicate the type of sequence (protein, transcript, genomic, etc.) that your Input Sequence should be BLASTed against. Then choose a BLAST Program to query your Input Sequence with and the Organism (genome) to use in your query.

Paste one Input Sequence in the text box. Only one sequence up to 31 Kb can be searched.

Default settings are indicated for the Expectation value, Maximum descriptions/alignments (V=B), and low complexity filter parameters.

BLAST Programs:
blastp compares an amino acid Input Sequence against a protein sequence database;
blastn compares a nucleotide Input Sequence against a nucleotide sequence database;
blastx compares the six-frame conceptual translation products of a nucleotide Input Sequence (both strands) against a protein sequence database;
tblastn compares a protein Input Sequence against a nucleotide sequence database dynamically translated in all six reading frames (both strands);
tblastx compares the six-frame translations of a nucleotide Input Sequence against the six-frame translations of a nucleotide sequence database.

transcript.displayName: Protein Motif Pattern
transcript.description:
Find genes whose protein product contains a motif pattern that you specify.
First choose the Organism that you wish to query. Then define the motif to query by entering a Perl-style regular expression that defines the motif you want to find. Regular expressions are more powerful than PROSITE patterns.

For example, "CC6+RK" is a Perl style regular expression representing "two cysteines followed by one or more hydrophobic amino acids, followed by arginine and then lysine". This type of search pattern allows you to find sequences that may be less well conserved.

Another example is the pattern of the Pexel motif, which can be represented as "RXLX[EQD]", meaning "an arginine, then any amino acid, then a leucine, then any amino acid, then either an aspartic acid, a glutamic acid, or a glutamine". Note that the period (.) is used to search for any character, even a non-amino acid character like J or asterisk (*). Thus, the search pattern "S.T" could find "SWT" or "S*T" or "S-T".

For a description of how to create regular expressions, please see the Regular Expression Tutorial.

The following codes can be used to represent classes of amino acids.
AA property Amino acids Code
Acidic DE 0
Alcohol ST 1
Aliphatic ILV 2
Aromatic FHWY 3
Basic KRH 4
Charged DEHKR 5
Hydrophobic AVILMFYW 6
Hydrophilic KRHDENQ 7
Polar CDEHKNQRST 8
Small ACDGNPSTV 9
Tiny AGS B
Turnlike ACDEGHKNQRST Z
Any ACDEFGHIKLM
NPQRSTVWY 		X

First choose the Organism(s) and Domain Database that you wish to query.

Then use either the 'Domain' or the 'Domain wildcard search' parameter to indicate the protein domain you wish to find.

When using the 'Specific Domain (s)' parameter, begin typing a domain name, accession or description, to see a list of all possible domains that match what you have typed. Then choose a domain name from the list. You can choose multiple domains using CTRL- or CMD-click when choosing the domains.

The domain matches to protein sequence are determined using the InterProScan program. To learn more about InterPro see the InterPro tutorial.

Find genes based on the Gene Ontology (GO) Term(s) or ID(s) assigned to them. GO annotations were either provided by the sequencing and annotation centers or inferred based on similarity to protein domains from the InterPro databases.

The Gene Ontology standardizes the representation of gene and gene product attributes across species and databases. The ontologies are a controlled vocabulary of terms for describing the molecular function, biological process and subcellular location of a gene product. This search returns genes with the GO Term or ID that you specify, as well as genes with terms that are specializations of your term (is-a). You may use '*' as a wild card character. For a list of GO terms, try the AmiGO browser.

When using the GO Subsets parameter selecting GO Slim generic will limit the search to GO terms that are part of the GO Slim generic ontology subset. To run on all available GO terms please select All GO terms.

When using the 'GO Term or GO ID' parameter, begin typing a GO Term or ID see a list of all possible GO categories that match what you have typed. Then choose a GO category from the list. You can choose multiple domains using CTRL- or CMD-click when choosing the domains.

When using the 'Free Text (use'*' for wildcard)' parameter, type the text term you wish to find and include an asterisk wildcard for ambiguous portions of your text term. (*ase, kin*, *kinase*) The search will query for all terms or IDs whose names, accessions or descriptions contain your text.
transcript.summary: Find genes based on the Gene Ontology (GO) Term(s) or ID(s) assigned to them.

transcript.displayName: Orthology Phylogenetic Profile
transcript.description:
Find genes that have a specified orthology-based phylogenetic profile. The phylogenetic profile of a gene is a series of "present" or "absent" calls, reflecting the inclusion of a gene in ortholog groups determined by the OrthoMCL algorithm.

The OrthoMCL algorithm clusters proteins into ortholog groups based on BLAST similarity across at least 150 genomes that span the tree of life. The ortholog groups document protein similarity across many species. Mapping ortholog groups onto the phyletic tree of life provides a framework for correlating protein similarity across species. The other species that are included in that gene's ortholog group can be thought of as a phylogenetic profile.

Use this search to define a pattern across those ortholog groups, and find genes that match that pattern. The pattern is a specification, for each species, of "include", "exclude", or "no constraints." Click on the radio button next to a species to toggle through the three states. A means "include", an means "exclude" and means "no constraints".

For example, to find genes that are present in Apicomplexa but not in humans, click on Apicomplexa until you see a and click on Homo sapiens until you see an .
transcript.summary: Find genes that have an orthology-based phylogenetic profile that you specify.

transcript.displayName: Text (product name, notes, etc.)
transcript.description:
Find genes by searching text annotations. The search compares your term against the text in the fields you specify, returning genes that have a match.

Select the Organism(s) you wish to query and enter your text term. Surround your text term with quotation marks to find exact phrase matches. For example, searching "ABC transporter" will match the exact phrase 'ABC transporter', whereas searching ABC transporter will match ABC and/or transporter. Use an asterisk (*) as a wild card character when looking for plural or compound words. For example, to find all compound words that start with phospho (ie. phosphodiesterase), type phospho* in the search window.

Hints: The search is similar to Google -- if you enter multiple words, genes that match more of those words will have a better score than those that match fewer of the words. If the words are found close together, that also improves the score. Higher scores appear at the top of your result list.

Looking for a list of genes?: If you need to query for a list of gene and you have each gene's ID, use the Identify Genes based on List of IDs search categorized under Genes, Annotation curation and identifiers, List of IDs.

Note about non-relevant results: Depending on how you configure it, this text search may return "non-relevant" genes (false positives). The search mechanically matches the term you supply against the Fields that you choose. The presence of your term in that field does not necessarily mean that the term actually describes the gene. The term may be mentioned in that field for less relevant reasons. To work around this, please carefully choose the Fields you want to search, and then, before drawing any conclusions, review the reference to your term in all matched fields in the gene page to confirm the meaning of its mention. The "Gene product" field is the most stringent and is unlikely to return false positives.
transcript.summary: Find genes with a text search against their product name, notes, GO, EC, Domains, NRDB, or metabolic pathways.

transcript.displayName: TF Binding Site Evidence
transcript.description:
The DNA sequence motifs bound by each ApiAP2 transcription factor were derived from protein binding microarray data using P. falciparum AP2 domains. Protein binding microarrays are non-organism specific and contain matches to all contiguous 10-mers at least once and non-palindromic 8-mers up to 32 times. The DNA motifs were determined using purified recombinant AP2 domains and the resulting position weight matrix for each AP2 domain was used to search upstream regions for significant matches. The AP2 domain that binds to each motif is indicated at the end of the gene ID. Binding sites are based on sequence matches only and have not been verified in vivo.
For further information, contact Manuel Llinas: manuel@princeton.edu

References:

Identification and genome-wide mapping of DNA binding specificities for the ApiAP2 family of regulators from the malaria parasite.Manuscript submitted. 2010 Campbell et al

Compact, universal DNA microarrays to comprehensively determine transcription-factor binding site specificities

The AP2 motifs were mapped to the genome using the algorithm described in the following paper: Identification of transcription factor binding sites in the human genome sequence
The P value is the probability that the binding site with that score would match at that position given the input DNA (intergenic and telomeric regions). For example, a P value of 1X10-4 means that you would find a good match every 10,000 base pairs on average on that strand.
transcript.summary: Find Genes which have a specified transcription factor binding site upstream or dowstream.

transcript.displayName: P. falciparum 3D7 Dual transcriptomes of malaria-infected Gambian children (RNA-Seq) WGCNA modules (functional prediction)
transcript.shortDisplayName: Pfal Gambian children RNA-Seq WGCNA modules
transcript.description:
Run this search: This search returns genes that belong to a specific WGCNA module. Choose your module of interest from the dropdown menu for the WGCNA Module parameter. (See the study explorer section below for tools on identifying a module that may be of interest to you.) Then choose the correlation coefficient that a gene's expression profile must share with the eigengene for the gene to be considered a member of the module. Click Get Answer to retrieve genes that meet your criteria.

WGCNA module: Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identifies groups of genes that have similar expression across samples. The analysis considers the whole transcriptome data set and clusters co-expressed genes into groups called modules. The modules in VEuPathDB were found using an iterative Weighted Gene Correlation Network Analysis.

Eigengene: The eigengene is created in the WGCNA analysis and is an imaginary gene whose expression profile represents an average gene within the module. Each module is represented by an eigengene. It is very likely that no gene within the module has the same expression profile as the eigengene.

Study Explorer: Relationships between modules or between modules and study variables such as participant disease status (asymptomatic vs severe), blood parasitemia, or age, may reveal central players in biological processes associated with the whole transcriptome data set. Use the Study Explorer to browse variable distributions, analyze/visualize correlations between modules, and analyze/visualize correlations between modules and study variables.
transcript.summary: Return genes within a module found in a weighted gene correlation network analysis.

The search will query two genomic regions that are equal in size to your Maximum Distance - one region on each side of the chromosome. The search returns genes found within the two regions.

transcript.displayName: Y2H Protein Interaction
transcript.description:
Find interacting partners of a specific gene as determined by yeast two-hybrid experiments. This data is available for P. falciparum only.

Gene ID
Enter the ID of the gene for which you want to find interaction partners. Genes returned by this search have protein products that were identified as interacting with the protein product of the Gene ID you enter here.

Number of searches that found this interaction
Indicate the number of independent yeast two-hybrid screens in which a given interaction was found before a gene (the interacting partner) is returned by the search. This parameter can also be considered "Times Reproduced". Interactions found in more than one yeast two-hybrid screen are more likely to be true positives because the data were independently produced.

Number of times this interaction was found Indicate the total number of times a given interaction was identified in all yeast two-hybrid screens before a gene (the interacting partner) is returned by the search. This parameter can also be considered "Times Observed".

An interaction can be identified multiple times in the same screen for several reasons (see 1-3 below) but only (3) provides independent confirmation of a putative interaction.
(1) The original yeast cell containing the pair of interacting proteins divided before being plated on selective media;
(2) The same prey plasmid was present in the library multiple times giving rise to multiple positive colonies;
(3) The prey gene was present in the library as multiple independent, overlapping fragments, all of which interact with a given bait.

Specified protein is bait or prey
Indicate whether the protein product of the Gene ID should be the bait (fused to the binding domain) or prey (fused to the activation domain) in the yeast two-hybrid experiment.
transcript.summary: Find interacting partners of a specific gene as determined by yeast two-hybrid experiments.

For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference.

transcript.displayName: P.f. eQTL HB3-Dd2 cross (similarity of associations)
transcript.description:
Find P. falciparum genes that have associations (cis or trans) to any/all the regions associated with the entered gene based on eQTL experiments on HB3,Dd2 and progeny. This query first looks for regions associated to the entered gene within the LOD cut-off and then finds other genes (across the genome) that are associated to these regions.

Microsatellites were mapped to the genomic sequence to generate a physical map with coordinates for the haplotype blocks. Since the exact coordinate location of cross-over event is unknown, two sets of locations were generated for the boundary of each of the haplotype block. A Conservative estimate for the boundary of a haplotype block starts at the first microsatellite to map within the region and ends at the last microsatellite to map in the region. A Liberal estimate of the boundary starts at the end of the last microsatellite that was mapped in the previous haplotype block and ends at the beginning of the first microsatellite mapped in the next haplotype block.(Refer to the picture below for a graphical explanation HB=Haplotype Block).



In this study, genome-wide expression level polymorphisms (ELPs) were examined in a genetic cross between phenotypically distinct parasite clones of P. falciparum (HB3 and Dd2). Using cDNA microarray hybridizations from the progeny of a genetic cross, gene expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) were mapped in an experimental population of malaria parasites. Each gene's transcript level was used as a segregating phenotype to identify regions of the Plasmodium genome dictating transcriptional variation.
transcript.summary: Find P. falciparum genes that have associations (cis or trans) to any/all the regions associated with the entered gene based on eQTL experiments on HB3,Dd2 and progeny.

transcript.displayName: Copy Number (CNV)
transcript.description:
Find genes with a copy number in a resequenced strain that is within a range that you specify.

Whole genome resequencing data was used to estimate each gene's copy number in resequenced strains. This search returns genes that are present at copy numbers (haploid number or gene dose) within a range that you specify.

You have the choice between two different metrics for defining copy number: haploid number or gene dose. Haploid number is the number of genes on an individual chromosome. Gene dose is the total number of genes in an organism, accounting for copy number of the chromosome. For example, a single-copy gene in a diploid organism has a haploid number of 1 and a gene dose of 2. You can choose to search for genes where at least one of your selected isolates meets your cutoff criteria for the chosen metric (By Strain/Sample), or where the median of the chosen metric across all the selected isolates meets the cutoff (Median of Selected Strains/Samples)

Begin by choosing an Organism (reference genome) and one or more resequenced isolates. Choose whether you want to apply your search criteris to individual samples or to the median of your chosen samples. Then choose your Metric, Operator and Copy Number, and initiate the search by clicking the GET ANSWER button. Genes returned by the search will have a copy number based on your chosen metric within the range that you specified. For example, searching with the haploid number equal to 4 will return genes with 4 copies on a chromosome.
transcript.summary: Find genes based on the number of copies in resequenced strains

transcript.displayName: Copy Number Comparison (CNV)
transcript.description:
Find genes by comparing the gene copy number in one or more resequenced strains to its copy number in the reference genome.

Whole genome resequencing was used to estimate each gene's copy number in resequenced strains. This search compares the estimated copy number of a gene in the resequenced strain with the copy number in the reference annotation. The copy number in the reference annotation is calculated as the number of genes that are both on the same chromosome and in the same ortholog group as the gene of interest. We infer that these genes have arisen as a result of tandem duplication of a common ancestor.

In this search, the metric for copy number is the haploid number, which is the number of copies of a gene on a single chromosome.

Begin by choosing an Organism (reference genome), and one or more resequenced strains, then choose how you want to compare the resequenced strains to the reference. You can search for genes where the estimated copy number in the resequenced strains is greater than or equal to, equal to, or less than or equal to the number of copies in the reference genome. You can choose to search for genes where at least one of your selected strains meets your chosen criteria (By Strain/Sample), or where the median across all your selected strains meets the criteria (Median of Selected Strains/Samples) After making your selections, initiate the search by clicking on the GET ANSWER button.

Be cautious using the less than or equal to operator, because regions which do not sequence well may appear to have reductions in gene copy number.
transcript.summary:
Find genes by comparing the gene copy number in the resequenced strain to its copy
                 number in the reference genome.

transcript.displayName: P. falciparum 3D7 Polysomal and steady-state asexual stage transcriptomes RNA-Seq (fold change)
transcript.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads mapped to each gene. First choose an Experiment since the available samples may change between experiments. If there is only one Experiment shown, this field will be selected for you.

Set the directionality of change in expression that you would like to see in the genes returned by this search. Choose to search for up-regulated, down-regulated, or up- and down-regulated genes.

Use the Fold Change >= parameter to set the cutoff for the change in expression for the genes returned by the search.

Choose the samples that you wish to compare. You may choose one or more samples for the reference and comparison. Fold change is calculated between your chosen reference and comparison samples and no statistical analysis is applied. For up-regulated genes the comparison/reference ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For down-regulated genes the reference/comparison ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference. There is an option to search for both up- and down- regulated genes in one query.

After selecting samples you have the option to perform the fold change calulation with the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further.

Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads mapped to each gene. First choose an Experiment since the available samples may change between experiments. If there is only one Experiment shown, this field will be selected for you.

Set the directionality of change in expression that you would like to see in the genes returned by this search. Choose to search for up-regulated, down-regulated, or up- and down-regulated genes.

Use the Fold Change >= parameter to set the cutoff for the change in expression for the genes returned by the search.

Choose the samples that you wish to compare. You may choose one or more samples for the reference and comparison. Fold change is calculated between your chosen reference and comparison samples and no statistical analysis is applied. For up-regulated genes the comparison/reference ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For down-regulated genes the reference/comparison ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference. There is an option to search for both up- and down- regulated genes in one query.

After selecting samples you have the option to perform the fold change calulation with the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further.
transcript.summary: Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment.

dynamicAttributes.name: fold_change_chosen_display
dynamicAttributes.help: * indicates that the chosen Ref or Comp values were subjected to the floor (which was set on the previous page) in order to compute the fold change.

dynamicAttributes.name: fold_change_chosen
dynamicAttributes.help: Chosen values less than the floor (which was set on the previous page) have been floored in order to compute the fold change.

dynamicAttributes.name: chose_group_one
dynamicAttributes.help: This number represents the expression value calculated for the 'Comparison Samples' and 'Operation Applied to Comparison Samples' that you chose when setting up the fold change search. If the value is lower than the floor, then the floor value is shown in parentheses and was used in the fold-change calculation.

dynamicAttributes.name: chose_group_two
dynamicAttributes.help: This number represents the expression value calculated for the 'Reference Samples' and 'Operation Applied to Reference Samples' that you chose when setting up the fold change search. If the value is lower than the floor, then the floor value is shown in parentheses and is used in the fold-change calculation.

dynamicAttributes.name: wdk_weight
dynamicAttributes.help: The *search result weight*. This is the sum of the weights you specified for individual searches that found this record.   The more searches that found this record the higher will be its weight.  To give a search a weight, click "Use Weights" on the search page, and provide the desired weight.

transcript.displayName: P. falciparum 3D7 Intraerythrocytic development cycle transcriptome (2019) RNA-Seq (fold change)
transcript.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads mapped to each gene. First choose an Experiment since the available samples may change between experiments. If there is only one Experiment shown, this field will be selected for you.

Set the directionality of change in expression that you would like to see in the genes returned by this search. Choose to search for up-regulated, down-regulated, or up- and down-regulated genes.

Use the Fold Change >= parameter to set the cutoff for the change in expression for the genes returned by the search.

Choose the samples that you wish to compare. You may choose one or more samples for the reference and comparison. Fold change is calculated between your chosen reference and comparison samples and no statistical analysis is applied. For up-regulated genes the comparison/reference ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For down-regulated genes the reference/comparison ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference. There is an option to search for both up- and down- regulated genes in one query.

After selecting samples you have the option to perform the fold change calulation with the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further.

transcript.displayName: P. berghei ANKA Transcriptomes of viable ApiAP2 mutants by directional RNA-seq RNA-Seq (fold change)
transcript.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads mapped to each gene. First choose an Experiment since the available samples may change between experiments. If there is only one Experiment shown, this field will be selected for you.

Set the directionality of change in expression that you would like to see in the genes returned by this search. Choose to search for up-regulated, down-regulated, or up- and down-regulated genes.

Use the Fold Change >= parameter to set the cutoff for the change in expression for the genes returned by the search.

Choose the samples that you wish to compare. You may choose one or more samples for the reference and comparison. Fold change is calculated between your chosen reference and comparison samples and no statistical analysis is applied. For up-regulated genes the comparison/reference ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For down-regulated genes the reference/comparison ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference. There is an option to search for both up- and down- regulated genes in one query.

After selecting samples you have the option to perform the fold change calulation with the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further.
transcript.summary: Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment.

dynamicAttributes.name: fold_change_chosen_display
dynamicAttributes.help: * indicates that the chosen Ref or Comp values were subjected to the floor (which was set on the previous page) in order to compute the fold change.

dynamicAttributes.name: fold_change_chosen
dynamicAttributes.help: Chosen values less than the floor (which was set on the previous page) have been floored in order to compute the fold change.

dynamicAttributes.name: chose_group_one
dynamicAttributes.help: This number represents the expression value calculated for the 'Comparison Samples' and 'Operation Applied to Comparison Samples' that you chose when setting up the fold change search. If the value is lower than the floor, then the floor value is shown in parentheses and was used in the fold-change calculation.

dynamicAttributes.name: chose_group_two
dynamicAttributes.help: This number represents the expression value calculated for the 'Reference Samples' and 'Operation Applied to Reference Samples' that you chose when setting up the fold change search. If the value is lower than the floor, then the floor value is shown in parentheses and is used in the fold-change calculation.

dynamicAttributes.name: wdk_weight
dynamicAttributes.help: The *search result weight*. This is the sum of the weights you specified for individual searches that found this record.   The more searches that found this record the higher will be its weight.  To give a search a weight, click "Use Weights" on the search page, and provide the desired weight.

formats.description: Display a histogram of weight distribution

transcript.displayName: P. falciparum 3D7 Transcriptome in severe vs uncomplicated malaria RNA-Seq (Differential Expression)
transcript.description:
Find genes that are differentially expressed between two groups of samples in an RNA-Seq experiment. This search uses a guided notebook within ${projectName} that runs DESeq2, a widely-used statistical method for RNA-Seq differential expression analysis (Love et al., 2014).

How to run this search: Open the Configure Search tab and work through the notebook steps in order:
  • Select Expression Data — Choose the gene identifier variable and count type for the dataset.
  • Explore Sample Variation (optional) — Run a PCA to visualise sources of variation across samples. Use it to spot outliers or batch effects and exclude them before the DESeq2 step.
  • Define Sample Groups — Select a metadata variable (e.g. treatment, tissue type, or developmental stage) and assign samples to a Reference group and a Comparison group.
  • Set Thresholds — Explore the results on an interactive volcano plot. Adjust the effect size and p-value thresholds to highlight the genes you want to retrieve.
  • Run the Search — Click Get Answer to retrieve all genes that meet your criteria.

Effect size: The effect size is expressed as a log2 fold change — how much more or less a gene is expressed in the Comparison group relative to the Reference group. A positive value indicates up-regulation; a negative value indicates down-regulation.

P-value: DESeq2 computes both a raw p-value and a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value for each gene. The volcano plot is drawn using the raw p-value (on a −log10 scale), and the p-value threshold you set on the plot is also applied to the raw p-value. Adjusted p-values are available in the mouse-over tooltip for each point on the volcano plot. A lower p-value (raw or adjusted) indicates a more statistically confident call.

Removing outliers: If the PCA plot reveals samples that cluster away from the rest (potential outliers or contaminated libraries), you can exclude them using the Select Samples step at the top of the notebook. Apply a filter on the sample identifier or a metadata variable to remove those samples before running DESeq2. Note that changing the sample subset will reset any group assignments you have already made in the DESeq2 step, so it is best to check the PCA first before defining your groups.

Find genes that are differentially expressed between two groups of samples in an RNA-Seq experiment. This search uses a guided notebook within ${projectName} that runs DESeq2, a widely-used statistical method for RNA-Seq differential expression analysis (Love et al., 2014).

How to run this search: Open the Configure Search tab and work through the notebook steps in order:
  • Select Expression Data — Choose the gene identifier variable and count type for the dataset.
  • Explore Sample Variation (optional) — Run a PCA to visualise sources of variation across samples. Use it to spot outliers or batch effects and exclude them before the DESeq2 step.
  • Define Sample Groups — Select a metadata variable (e.g. treatment, tissue type, or developmental stage) and assign samples to a Reference group and a Comparison group.
  • Set Thresholds — Explore the results on an interactive volcano plot. Adjust the effect size and p-value thresholds to highlight the genes you want to retrieve.
  • Run the Search — Click Get Answer to retrieve all genes that meet your criteria.

Effect size: The effect size is expressed as a log2 fold change — how much more or less a gene is expressed in the Comparison group relative to the Reference group. A positive value indicates up-regulation; a negative value indicates down-regulation.

P-value: DESeq2 computes both a raw p-value and a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value for each gene. The volcano plot is drawn using the raw p-value (on a −log10 scale), and the p-value threshold you set on the plot is also applied to the raw p-value. Adjusted p-values are available in the mouse-over tooltip for each point on the volcano plot. A lower p-value (raw or adjusted) indicates a more statistically confident call.

Removing outliers: If the PCA plot reveals samples that cluster away from the rest (potential outliers or contaminated libraries), you can exclude them using the Select Samples step at the top of the notebook. Apply a filter on the sample identifier or a metadata variable to remove those samples before running DESeq2. Note that changing the sample subset will reset any group assignments you have already made in the DESeq2 step, so it is best to check the PCA first before defining your groups.

transcript.displayName: P. vinckei vinckei CY Life cycle stage transcriptome for P. vinckei lentum RNA-Seq (Differential Expression)
transcript.description:
Find genes that are differentially expressed between two groups of samples in an RNA-Seq experiment. This search uses a guided notebook within ${projectName} that runs DESeq2, a widely-used statistical method for RNA-Seq differential expression analysis (Love et al., 2014).

How to run this search: Open the Configure Search tab and work through the notebook steps in order:
  • Select Expression Data — Choose the gene identifier variable and count type for the dataset.
  • Explore Sample Variation (optional) — Run a PCA to visualise sources of variation across samples. Use it to spot outliers or batch effects and exclude them before the DESeq2 step.
  • Define Sample Groups — Select a metadata variable (e.g. treatment, tissue type, or developmental stage) and assign samples to a Reference group and a Comparison group.
  • Set Thresholds — Explore the results on an interactive volcano plot. Adjust the effect size and p-value thresholds to highlight the genes you want to retrieve.
  • Run the Search — Click Get Answer to retrieve all genes that meet your criteria.

Effect size: The effect size is expressed as a log2 fold change — how much more or less a gene is expressed in the Comparison group relative to the Reference group. A positive value indicates up-regulation; a negative value indicates down-regulation.

P-value: DESeq2 computes both a raw p-value and a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value for each gene. The volcano plot is drawn using the raw p-value (on a −log10 scale), and the p-value threshold you set on the plot is also applied to the raw p-value. Adjusted p-values are available in the mouse-over tooltip for each point on the volcano plot. A lower p-value (raw or adjusted) indicates a more statistically confident call.

Removing outliers: If the PCA plot reveals samples that cluster away from the rest (potential outliers or contaminated libraries), you can exclude them using the Select Samples step at the top of the notebook. Apply a filter on the sample identifier or a metadata variable to remove those samples before running DESeq2. Note that changing the sample subset will reset any group assignments you have already made in the DESeq2 step, so it is best to check the PCA first before defining your groups.

transcript.displayName: P. falciparum 3D7 Transcriptome in severe vs uncomplicated malaria changes in sense and antisense transcripts
transcript.description:
Find genes that exhibit simultaneous changes in sense and antisense transcripts in the Comparison sample relative to the Reference Sample. For example, you could look for genes showing increasing antisense transcripts and decreasing sense transcripts, as might occur when antisense transcription suppresses sense transcription. The search will perform all pairwise comparisons between the chosen Comparison samples and the chosen Reference samples. Below is an example where there is an increase in antisense transcripts and a decrease in sense transcripts in the Comparison sample:



An example of the TPM data for a gene is shown below. You can select the direction and the magnitude of change for the sense and antisense transcripts.



The results page lists the genes, along with each pair of samples (Reference->Comparison), that meet the criteria. The results page also shows a graph depicting all pairwise fold-changes in antisense and sense transcripts that is useful in identifying which samples meet the criteria that you selected AND whether this pattern is observed across all samples.



Each point shows the sense fold-change and the antisense fold-change between a pair of samples. A point on the red dotted diagonal line represents a pair of samples where the antisense fold-change and the sense fold-change are the same. Sample pairs that meet the fold-change critera are represented by points located within the corner of the graph that is closed off with a vertical and a horizontal red dotted line. (Note that some pairs meet the fold-change criteria but do not meet the change in antisense fraction, which is an advanced parameter. If you want to identify more genes, then you should decrease the value of this parameter.) On the Results page, you can click on the graph to open a new browser window containing an enlarged graph. The enlarged graph can be moused-over to show which sample comparison is represented by each point.
transcript.summary: Find genes with specific patterns of sense and antisense transcripts, using evidence from strand-specific RNA-Seq data

transcript.displayName: P. vivax P01 Hypnozoite RNA-Seq changes in sense and antisense transcripts
transcript.description:
Find genes that exhibit simultaneous changes in sense and antisense transcripts in the Comparison sample relative to the Reference Sample. For example, you could look for genes showing increasing antisense transcripts and decreasing sense transcripts, as might occur when antisense transcription suppresses sense transcription. The search will perform all pairwise comparisons between the chosen Comparison samples and the chosen Reference samples. Below is an example where there is an increase in antisense transcripts and a decrease in sense transcripts in the Comparison sample:



An example of the TPM data for a gene is shown below. You can select the direction and the magnitude of change for the sense and antisense transcripts.



The results page lists the genes, along with each pair of samples (Reference->Comparison), that meet the criteria. The results page also shows a graph depicting all pairwise fold-changes in antisense and sense transcripts that is useful in identifying which samples meet the criteria that you selected AND whether this pattern is observed across all samples.



Each point shows the sense fold-change and the antisense fold-change between a pair of samples. A point on the red dotted diagonal line represents a pair of samples where the antisense fold-change and the sense fold-change are the same. Sample pairs that meet the fold-change critera are represented by points located within the corner of the graph that is closed off with a vertical and a horizontal red dotted line. (Note that some pairs meet the fold-change criteria but do not meet the change in antisense fraction, which is an advanced parameter. If you want to identify more genes, then you should decrease the value of this parameter.) On the Results page, you can click on the graph to open a new browser window containing an enlarged graph. The enlarged graph can be moused-over to show which sample comparison is represented by each point.

For example, you could look for genes showing increasing antisense transcripts and decreasing sense transcripts, as might occur when antisense transcription suppresses sense transcription. The search will perform all pairwise comparisons between the chosen Comparison samples and the chosen Reference samples. Below is an example where there is an increase in antisense transcripts and a decrease in sense transcripts in the Comparison sample:



An example of the TPM data for a gene is shown below. You can select the direction and the magnitude of change for the sense and antisense transcripts.



The results page lists the genes, along with each pair of samples (Reference->Comparison), that meet the criteria. The results page also shows a graph depicting all pairwise fold-changes in antisense and sense transcripts that is useful in identifying which samples meet the criteria that you selected AND whether this pattern is observed across all samples.



Each point shows the sense fold-change and the antisense fold-change between a pair of samples. A point on the red dotted diagonal line represents a pair of samples where the antisense fold-change and the sense fold-change are the same. Sample pairs that meet the fold-change critera are represented by points located within the corner of the graph that is closed off with a vertical and a horizontal red dotted line. (Note that some pairs meet the fold-change criteria but do not meet the change in antisense fraction, which is an advanced parameter. If you want to identify more genes, then you should decrease the value of this parameter.) On the Results page, you can click on the graph to open a new browser window containing an enlarged graph. The enlarged graph can be moused-over to show which sample comparison is represented by each point.

transcript.displayName: RNA-Seq Fold Chg (User Datasets)
transcript.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an RNA-Seq experiment. First choose an experiment as the available samples may change. If only one "Experiment" is shown, this field will be selected for you.

After selecting samples you have the option to take the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further. Finally, you can choose the directionality and the magnitude of the difference. transcript.displayName: Transform by Orthology
transcript.description:
Find the PlasmoDB genes that are orthologs (or paralogs) of the genes in a search result. The typical use of this query is to begin by having an interesting result in a strategy. Then, use this search to find orthologs of those genes in a species that may not be annotated with the data from your original result. In general, use this search to transform sets of genes from one species to others.

Ortholog groups were generated from more than 100 species using OrthoMCL as described in Li L, Stoeckert CJ Jr, Roos DS. OrthoMCL: identification of ortholog groups for eukaryotic genomes. Genome Res. 2003 13:2178-89. The OrthoMCL DB site is described in Chen F. Mackey AJ. Stoeckert CJ Jr. Roos DS. OrthoMCL-DB: querying a comprehensive multi-species collection of ortholog groups. NAR. 34(Database issue):D363-8.

genomic-sequence.description:
Find genomic sequences or chromosomes based on their estimated copy number in resequenced strains.

Whole genome resequencing data was used to estimate the copy number (ploidy) of genomic sequences in the resequenced strains. This search returns genomic sequences or chromosomes with an estimated copy number greater than or equal to a value that you specify in at least one of the chosen samples. Begin by choosing an Organism (reference genome). Next choose one or more strains or samples that have been mapped against the chosen reference. Choose whether you want to search for genomic sequences where the group median for the selection strains/samples meets the Copy Number criteria (Median) or whether you want at least one of the strains/samples in the group to meet the Copy Number criteria (By Sample). Then enter a value for Copy Number and initiate the search by clicking the GET ANSWER button.

Genomic sequences returned by the search will have either have a median estimated copy number greater than or equal to the value you entered for the Copy Number across the selected strains/samples, or will have an estimated copy number greater than or equal to the value you entered for the Copy Number in at least one of the selected strains/samples. For example, to find supernumerary chromosomes in a diploid organism, search for genomic sequences where the Copy Number is >= 3.
genomic-sequence.summary: Find genomic sequences or chromosomes based on the number of copies in the genome.

genomic-segment.displayName: P.f. eQTL HB3-Dd2 cross (segments by association to genes)
genomic-segment.description:
Find genomic segments that have associations with the entered gene(s) based on eQTL experiments on HB3, Dd2 and progeny.

Microsatellites were mapped to the genomic sequence to generate a physical map with co-ordinates for the haplotype blocks. Since the exact co- ordinate location of cross-over event is unknown, two sets of locations were generated for the boundary of each of the haplotype block. A Conse rvative estimate for the boundary of a haplotype block starts at the first microsatellite to map within the region and ends at the last microsatellite to map in the region. A Liberal estimate of the boundary starts at the end of the last microsatellite that was mapped in the previous haplotype block and ends at the beginning of the first microsatellite mapped in the next haplotype block.(Refer to the picture below for a gr aphical explanation HB=Haplotype Block).



In this study, genome-wide expression level polymorphisms (ELPs) were examined in a genetic cross between phenotypically distinct parasite clo nes of P. falciparum (HB3 and Dd2). Using cDNA microarray hybridizations from the progeny of a genetic cross, gene expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) were mapped in an experimental population of malaria parasites. Each gene's transcript level was used as a segregating phenotype to identify regions of the Plasmodium genome dictating transcriptional variation.
For further details, please refer the following publication: Gonzales JM, Patel JJ, Ponm ee N, Jiang L, Tan A, et al. 2008 Regulatory Hotspots in the Malaria Parasite Genome Dictate Transcriptional Variation. PLoS Biol 6(9): e238. doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.0060238
genomic-segment.summary: Find genomic segments that have associations with the entered gene(s) based on eQTL experiments on HB3, Dd2 and progeny.

variation.displayName: SNV Differences Within a Group of Samples
variation.description:
This search analyzes whole genome sequencing data from a group of samples to find variants associated with the group.

Each sample's sequencing reads are aligned to the reference genome (Organism) and variants are recorded for each sample based on the Read Frequency Threshold. Then, scanning variant locations across the group of samples, variants are returned by the search if the Minor Allele Frequency and the Percent samples with a base call are met.

Organism: The Organism parameter defines the species of the samples and the genome in which the variants are determined. Choosing an Organism focuses the Samples parameter to the samples of that organism, changing the subset available when forming your group.

Samples: Sample sequences are accompanied by characteristics of the sample -- where it was collected, the host, alignment statistics. By default the group includes all samples from the Organism you chose; you may narrow the group using those characteristics. At least two samples are required, since polymorphism within a group of one is undefined.

Read frequency threshold: An allele is called for a sample at a location if that fraction of the sample's aligned reads support it. For example, a sample with 10 reads at a location -- 6 A and 4 C -- is called A at a threshold of 60% or less, and not called at 80%. This matters most for diploid or aneuploid organisms, where heterozygous positions are expected near 50%.

Minor allele frequency: Among the qualifying calls at a location, the minor allele frequency is the percent that are not the major allele. A location is returned if that is at or above the value you specify. Use 0 to find every variant location within the group.

Percent samples with a base call: A location is only considered if this fraction of your selected samples have a qualifying call there. With 20 samples and a threshold of 75%, a location with fewer than 15 called samples is ignored.
variation.summary:
Find SNVs that differ within a group of samples, with an option to
          specify minor allele frequency.

dynamicAttributes.name: PercentMinorAlleles
dynamicAttributes.help: Percent of minor alleles for this group of samples at this variant location (where 'minor allele' means any allele that is not the major allele).

dynamicAttributes.name: PercentIsolateCalls
dynamicAttributes.help: Percent of the samples at this variant location from the specified group that have read calls (over the threshold specified in the search)

dynamicAttributes.name: Phenotype
dynamicAttributes.help: 1 = this variant is within a gene and there is at least one sample in this set that has an allele with product that is non-synonymous with the most popular allele

Minor allele frequency: Among the qualifying calls at a location, the minor allele frequency is the percent that are not the major allele. Use 0 to find every variant location within the group.

variation.description:
This search analyzes whole genome sequencing data from a group of samples to find variants associated with the group, and returns only those falling within the genes you specify.

Each sample's sequencing reads are aligned to the reference genome (Organism) and variants are recorded for each sample based on the Read Frequency Threshold. Then, scanning variant locations within your genes across the group of samples, variants are returned if the Minor Allele Frequency and the Percent samples with a base call are met.

Genes: Your gene IDs are resolved to each gene's genomic span, and variants are returned by position within those spans. A variant in an intron or UTR of one of your genes is therefore returned, since the span covers the whole gene rather than only its coding sequence.

Organism: The Organism parameter defines the species of the samples and the genome in which the variants are determined. Choose the organism your genes belong to.

Samples: By default the group includes all samples from the Organism you chose; you may narrow it using the sample characteristics. At least two samples are required, since polymorphism within a group of one is undefined.

Read frequency threshold: An allele is called for a sample at a location if that fraction of the sample's aligned reads support it. This matters most for diploid or aneuploid organisms, where heterozygous positions are expected near 50%.

Minor allele frequency: Among the qualifying calls at a location, the minor allele frequency is the percent that are not the major allele. Use 0 to find every variant location within the group.

Percent samples with a base call: A location is only considered if this fraction of your selected samples have a qualifying call there.

Find SNVs located in a set of genes that differ within a group of samples,
          with an option to specify minor allele frequency.

variation.displayName: SNV Differences Between Two Groups of Samples
variation.description:
This search compares whole genome sequencing data from two groups of samples to find variants that differ between the two groups.

Each sample's sequencing reads are aligned to the reference genome (Organism) and variants are recorded for each sample based on the Read Frequency Threshold. Then, scanning locations across the samples in Set A and Set B separately, the major allele of each set is recorded where it meets that set's major allele frequency and percent samples with a base call. A location is returned when the two sets' major alleles differ.

Choosing the two groups: Set A and Set B must differ. Use the sample characteristics to define each group, for example samples from two different countries, or two different host phenotypes.

Major allele frequency: Among the qualifying calls at a location within one set, the major allele frequency is the percent carrying the most common allele. Unlike the within-group searches, 100% is permissible here and is the most stringent setting: the search identifies each set's major allele first and then compares the two, so demanding unanimity within a set is a sharper test rather than an impossible one. Lower the threshold to return more locations.

Read frequency threshold: An allele is called for a sample at a location if that fraction of the sample's aligned reads support it. Each set has its own threshold.

Percent samples with a base call: A location is only considered within a set if this fraction of that set's samples have a qualifying call there.
variation.summary:
Find SNVs that distinguish two groups of samples, based on the major
          allele threshold you supply for each group.

compound.description:
Find compounds with variation in metabolite levels. Note that when the compound has multiple isotopomers, the metabolite isotopomers levels were summed.

Infected RBCs were enriched using Percoll and parasites were isolated from infected RBCs with saponin. Intracellular metabolites were measured from pellets while secreted metabolites were measured from the media
Infected RBCs, isolated parasites, and uninfected RBCs were incubated for 4 hours in RPMI containing U-13 C glutamine at pH 6.4, 7.4, and 8.4. Extracts were analyzed by mass spectrometry. The effect of pH on steady-state metabolite levels and glutamine metabolism was measured.

Warning: all metabolite assignments provided in this alpha release should be treated as preliminary.
